source_text: Κἀγὼ οὖν προσδοκῶ ὑπό τινος τῶν ὠνομασμένων ἐπιβουλευθῆναι καὶ ξύλῳ ἐμπαγῆναι, ἢ κἂν ὑπὸ Κρίσκεντος τοῦ φιλοψόφου καὶ φιλοκόμπου. Οὐ γὰρ φιλόσοφον εἰπεῖν ἄξιον τὸν ἄνδρα, ὅς γε περὶ ἡμῶν ἃ μὴ ἐπίσταται δημοσίᾳ καταμαρτυρεῖ, ὡς ἀθέων καὶ ἀσεβῶν Χριστιανῶν ὄντων, πρὸς χάριν καὶ ἡδονὴν τῶν πολλῶν τῶν πεπλανημένων ταῦτα πράττων. Εἴτε γὰρ μὴ ἐντυχὼν τοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ διδάγμασι κατατρέχει ἡμῶν, παμπόνηρός ἐστι καὶ ἰδιωτῶν πολὺ χείρων, οἳ φυλάττονται πολλάκις περὶ ὧν οὐκ ἐπίστανται διαλέγεσθαι καὶ ψευδομαρτυρεῖν· ἢ εἰ ἐντυχών, μὴ συνῆκε τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς μεγαλεῖον ἢ συνεὶς πρὸς τὸ μὴ ὑποπτευθῆναι τοιοῦτος ταῦτα ποιεῖ, πολὺ μᾶλλον ἀγεννὴς καὶ παμπόνηρος, ἰδιωτικῆς καὶ ἀλόγου δόξης καὶ φόβου ἐλάττων ὤν. Καὶ γὰρ προσθέντα με καὶ ἐρωτήσαντα αὐτὸν ἐρωτήσεις τινὰς τοιαύτας καὶ μαθεῖν καὶ ἐλέγξαι, ὅτι ἀληθῶς μηδὲν ἐπίσταται, εἰδέναι ὑμᾶς βούλομαι. Καὶ ὅτι ἀληθῆ λέγω, εἰ μὴ ἀνηνέχθησαν ὑμῖν αἱ κοινωνίαι τῶν λόγων, ἕτοιμος καὶ ἐφ᾿ ὑμῶν κοινωνεῖν τῶν ἐρωτήσεων πάλιν· βασιλικὸν δ᾿ ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ἔργον εἴη. Εἰ δὲ καὶ ἐγνώσθησαν ὑμῖν αἱ ἐρωτησεις μου καὶ αἱ ἐκείνου ἀποκρίσεις, φανερὸν ὑμῖν ἐστιν, ὅτι οὐδὲν τῶν ἡμετέρων ἐπίσταται· ἢ εἰ καὶ ἐπίσταται, διὰ τοὺς ἀκούοντας δὲ οὐ τολμᾷ λέγειν ὁμοίως Σωρκάτει, ὡς προέφην, οὐ φιλόσοφος ἀλλὰ φιλόδοξος ἀνὴρ δείκνυται, ὅς γε μηδὲ τὸ σωκρατικὸν ἀξιέραστον ὂν τιμᾷ· Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε πρὸ τῆς ἀληθείας τιμητέος ἀνήρ“. Ἀδύνατον δὲ Κυνικῷ. ἀδιάφορον τὸ τέλος προθεμένῳ, τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἰδέναι πλὴν ἀδιαφορίας.
orientation: Justin, the author, is speaking in his own voice, explaining why he expects to be plotted against and why he considers the Cynic philosopher Crescens a slanderer rather than a true philosopher.
pass_a_gloss: And I therefore expect to be plotted against by one of those named and to be stuck on a stake, or at least by Crescens the lover of noise and lover of show. For it is not worthy to call the man a philosopher, who at least about us what he does not know publicly testifies against, as atheists and impious Christians being, for favor and pleasure of the many who have been deceived these things doing. For either if not having encountered the teachings of Christ he runs down us, he is utterly wicked and of laymen much worse, who guard often about what they do not know to talk and to bear false witness; or if having encountered, he did not understand the greatness in them or having understood in order not to be suspected such a one these things does, much more ignoble and utterly wicked, of layman's and irrational opinion and fear lesser being. For also having added me and having asked him questions some such and to learn and to refute, that truly nothing he knows, you to know I wish. And that true things I say, if not were reported to you the exchanges of the words, ready also before you to share of the questions again; royal and this work would be. But if also were known to you my questions and his answers, clear to you it is, that nothing of our things he knows; or if also he knows, because of the hearers but he does not dare to speak like Socrates, as I said before, not a philosopher but a lover of opinion man he is shown, who at least not even the Socratic, worthy of love being, honors: 'But not at all before the truth is a man to be honored.' Impossible but for a Cynic, indifference the end having set before, the good to know except indifference.

choices.english: to be stuck on a stake
choices.why: ξύλον is literally wood or a wooden stake; 'stuck on a stake' preserves the physical image of execution by impalement or crucifixion without importing a specific Roman penalty term
rejected: to be nailed to a cross

choices.english: lover of noise and lover of show
choices.why: The two compounds are parallel and mocking; rendering them as parallel 'lover of' phrases keeps the wordplay against φιλόσοφος (philosopher) visible

choices.term: πρὸς χάριν καὶ ἡδονὴν τῶν πολλῶν
choices.english: for favor and pleasure of the many
choices.why: χάρις and ἡδονή are distinct: favor (currying favor) and pleasure (gratifying); keeping both nouns preserves the double motive Justin alleges
rejected: to please and gratify the crowd
for the gratification of the masses

choices.why: ἰδιώτης means a private person or layman without specialized knowledge; 'laymen' keeps the contrast with the would-be philosopher
ἀγεννής means low-born or ignoble; 'ignoble' captures both the social and moral sense Justin intends
φιλόδοξος is literally lover of δόξα (opinion or reputation); 'lover of opinion' keeps the parallel with φιλόσοφος and the contrast with truth

pass_b_english: So I too expect to be plotted against by one of those I have named and nailed to a cross, or at least by Crescens, that lover of noise and show. For the man is not worthy to be called a philosopher, since he publicly testifies against us about things he does not understand, saying that Christians are atheists and impious, and he does this to win favor and pleasure from the many who have been deceived.

If he attacks us without having read the teachings of Christ, he is utterly wicked and far worse than ordinary people, who often guard themselves against discussing and bearing false witness about things they do not know. But if he has read them and did not grasp the greatness in them, or grasped it but acts this way so that he will not be suspected of being such a person, then he is far more ignoble and utterly wicked, being inferior to common irrational opinion and fear.

For I want you to know that I approached him and asked him certain questions of this kind, to learn from him and to prove that he truly knows nothing. And to show that I speak the truth, if the exchanges of our words have not been reported to you, I am ready to share in the questioning again even in your presence; and this too would be a work worthy of an emperor. But if my questions and his answers have become known to you, it is clear to you that he knows nothing of our teachings; or if he does know, but does not dare to speak because of his hearers, then, as I said before, he is shown to be not a philosopher but a lover of glory, since he does not even honor the Socratic saying, worthy of love as it is: "But no man is worthy of honor before the truth."
But it is impossible for a Cynic, who has set up indifference as his goal, to know the good except indifference.
notes: The source text has Σωρκάτει for Σωκράτει (Socrates), an apparent scribal error or variant spelling; glossed as Socrates. The quoted saying 'Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε πρὸ τῆς ἀληθείας τιμητέος ἀνήρ' appears to be a quotation or adaptation from Plato's Republic 595c, but the wording is not a direct scriptural citation.

fixed: The Greek φιλοψόφου καὶ φιλοκόμπου means 'lover of noise and lover of show' (φιλόψοφος = lover of noise, φιλόκομπος = lover of show/boasting). The English 'lover of noise and show' is a literal rendering, but the source does not mean a charlatan or self-promoter; it means someone who loves noise and display. The English is accurate to the source, so no edit is needed.
